utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to greet the parties and all those contributing to our trial. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Riad, Judge Wald, my colleagues. Good morning. I wanted to raise with the Court a correction in the record that I thought was important to make now, and it relates to the testimony of General Krstic on 31st of October, 2000. In his testimony, my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, asked General Krstic to read Prosecutor's Exhibit 467B, which was a Bosnian language handwritten copy of an order, and it -- what was read into the record was the following: "We wish to inform you --" I'm sorry. What was translated was the following: "We wish to inform you that we are able to ensure the presence of members of the command and representatives of the municipal authorities for the official farewell for General Zivanovic, the outgoing commander of the Drina Corps, on 23rd of June, 1995, at 1300 hours." The word "outgoing" was not correctly translated for -- as General Krstic was reading the document. The correct translation of the word that General Krstic read is "hitherto," and I want to insert -- bring Your Honours' attention to that point. The head of the Language Service Section, Maja Drazenovic-Carrieri, has reviewed the document again. She has filed, at my request, a core addendum. She has filed that with the Registrar's Office on the 1st of November, 2000. In addition, I have discussed this matter with my colleagues, and they have no disagreement with what I am saying in respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit 476 [sic] and the correct translation of that document. I wanted to bring that to Your Honours' attention before we conclude -- before we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Is that 467 or 476?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I said "476," I misspoke. It's 467, 467B, and the English language version is 467A. And the translation that was submitted is the correct translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Riad, Judge Wald. With your leave, Judge Riad, we can continue now with the cross-examination of Witness DA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DA. Mr. Cayley, the Prosecutor, will continue asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I think perhaps the witness cannot hear us. Can you ensure that his headphones are on the right channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we left off yesterday speaking about the indictment against Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. Now, I want to move ahead in time and I want you to think about the 12th of July of 1995, when I think you arrived at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the Vlasenica headquarters? Would it be between 1700 and 1800 hours in the early evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, around 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think when you arrived there, you stated that Colonel Jokic [phoen] was the duty officer in the Operations Centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jocic, and not Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. It's my pronunciation. And that was Colonel Predrag Jocic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think I'm correct in saying that you also saw Major Pajcic [phoen] and, for a brief period of time, General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Pajic, not Pajcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were a member of the Drina Corps staff for a considerable period of time, and you knew all of the members of the staff while you were working there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, on that evening, the other members of staff from the Command that you recall seeing. I'll simply do it like a shopping list and I'll ask you the names and you can say yes or no whether you recall seeing them in the headquarters. Now, the first officer is Colonel Milenko Lazic, who was the Chief of Operations of the Drina Corps. Was he at the headquarters on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic, the Operations officer from the former Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was he there on the evening of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Kosoric, was he in the headquarters on that evening? Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, you will recall, was the assistant within the Intelligence Department of the Drina Corps staff.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. I didn't see him -- no, I don't remember whether I saw him. I told you the people I remember seeing, because I was there very briefly, I was in a hurry to go to the Press Centre to have a bath because I was coming from the mountains, and it seems to me that I briefly saw the men and the names of the people I mentioned at the beginning; Jocic, Pajic, several soldiers from the Communications Centre, two of my associates from the Press Centre, and the Commander Zivanovic. That was it, as far as I can remember, but it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me try and refresh your memory with some names. As you know, a military headquarters is a busy place; people are moving around. If I give you the name, you might remember it. Major Pavle Golic, did you see him on the evening of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Pajo Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Mirko Petrovic -- I'm sorry, Lieutenant Mirko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Petrovic either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Radenko Jovicic? He was head of the Personnel and Administrative Section.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't drop in at his office; I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your boss, Colonel Cerovic, was he there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on sick leave at the time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Acamovic, he was the Assistant Commander for Rear Services, was he there on the 12th of July in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on the floor above. I didn't go to see them so I don't know whether he was in the Command or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, who you'll recall was the Transportation officer, was he in the headquarters on that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see Major Basevic, who was the Chief of Technical Services? Was he there on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All their offices were on the floor above so I didn't go there, I didn't have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Ljubo Sobot, he was the Chief of Rear Area Operations. Did you see him there on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sobot. I didn't see Sobot either. They were all on the floor above.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind, Witness, that people do move around within a military headquarters and don't constantly stay in their office. Lieutenant Marijanovic, who worked for Colonel Cerovic, I think he's dead now but he worked within your section.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he worked in the Legal Affairs Department. He was there. We did come across one another somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Nedo Blagojevic, he was the Chief of Communications for the Drina Corps. Was he in on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, and I don't know the first name of this individual, either Gasevic or Gavric, he was the assistant to the administrative officer, Lieutenant Colonel Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who you are referring to but I didn't see him. We didn't run into each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it Gavric or Gasevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gasevic. I don't remember his first name. He joined the Corps later. I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Ignjat Milanovic, was he in the headquarters on the 12th of July? You know him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Milanovic. I didn't see him at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was his job on the Staff; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was head of the Air Defence Service, I think it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Major Petrovic, who was the Commander of the Military Police Battalion of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were housed in a different building about 100 metres away from headquarters, and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was Major Ratko Tisma there? He was the Quartermaster.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Tisma either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel or Major Hendryk Jevicki, also working in the Quartermaster Department, do you recall anybody of that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him. He worked in the Quartermaster Service. I didn't see him in our building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lastly, did you see a military police officer by the name of Teso Tesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military police also was about 100 metres away from our building and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think I'm right in saying that that evening you spent at the Corps in Vlasenica, you stayed at the Corps in Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you stay that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my room, where I would regularly spend the night; though I spent most of my time in the Press Centre premises which were not in the same building as the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the room that you spent the night in was in the Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which floor was it on? Was it on the ground floor or first floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that a number of these officers worked on the first floor. Did you see any of them at all when you spent the night there? Did you have any contact with anybody other than the people that you've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As it was late, I had a shower, prepared clean clothing because I knew that, in the morning, I had to leave. I just exchanged a few words with my colleagues from the Press Centre, I called up my family -- we hadn't been in touch for some time -- and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the headquarters busy with work at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my sector, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The rest of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't have any insight. As I said, I spent very little time there. I didn't notice any particular haste among the people working there. They were doing their regular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you must have passed by the offices of these other staff officers and noticed whether people were moving around inside these offices, whether people were coming out of offices.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our custom not to move about too much around headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long had you been away for from the Vlasenica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been away for about ten days and more at the time. But anyway, I moved about frequently, so it was nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you had been away for ten days and you made absolutely no effort to have any contacts with any of these other officers within the headquarters, all people that you knew, all people that were your military colleagues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cerovic, who was my boss, was not there. General Zivanovic devoted very little time for his conversation with me. The only person I spoke to for a little longer was the late Marijanovic and my associates in the Press Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it not customary within military headquarters for staff officers to have contact with officers from other branches within the headquarters with whom they work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is customary to engage in regular, normal conversations. But you must understand: I came late. People wanted to rest. And I too had my own plans, that is, to have a shower and change, to call up my family. And time flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in essence, other than the officers that you mentioned, you had absolutely no sight or contact with any of the 18-odd staff officers that I've mentioned from the headquarters on that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only with the people I mentioned having seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now move to the 13th of July. In the morning you met General Krstic. Whereabouts did you meet General Krstic that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of his office, in front of the office of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Within the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the building of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What floor is the Chief of Staff's office located on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you came out of the room in which you had been sleeping and went straight to General Krstic's office on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the office, but the corridor in front of the office. It's about 50 metres away from my own office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And nobody else, I assume, was out in the corridor; it was completely empty, apart from General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who else was in the headquarters on that morning that you can recall? Was General Krstic there by himself in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Jocic was there still there. He still hadn't handed over his duties to the duty officer. Major Pajic. I asked -- I saw the cooks, the communications people who were going up to the restaurant and the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the only --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The only people you saw were General Krstic; the paymaster, Major Pajic; the duty officer, Colonel Jokic [phoen]; and then the cooks and some signallers. Those are the only people that you saw that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jocic. Yes, yes. That would be it. Yes. Those were the people that I saw. Because I was there for a brief space of time. I was in a hurry to get to Sokolac on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where was everybody else that morning, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Out of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them if they were -- unless they were in their offices. But as I say, I didn't go to the upper floor, because that was where the Rear Services were and the Traffic and Communication Department and the other services, up on the upper storey.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many floors are there in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Three or four?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on the evening of the 12th and the morning of the 13th, am I right in saying you were only on the ground floor and first floor; you limited yourself to those two floors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And in the neighbouring building, on the premises of the Press Centre. That was the area I moved around. It was an area of some -- a circumference of 100 metres, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To get from each floor there were a set of stairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Usually there's a link by means of stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in order for you to get from the ground floor to the first floor, you went up and down the stairs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, normally, in the normal way, customary way. How else would I move around?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the people on the third and fourth floor that were in the headquarters would also be using the staircase to go up and down the building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you were on the staircase, did you see any members of the staff of the headquarters, apart from the three officers that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting anyone. It wasn't usual for us to move around. The commander asked us to do our work without moving around the corridors and hallways much, except during lunchtime and dinnertime, when we had to go to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But I'm right in saying, am I not, Witness, that a staff headquarters works by the various bodies actually communicating with each other in the planning and execution of an operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if the directive from the commander was that you had to stay in your office except at lunchtime or dinner, how did you communicate with the other staff branches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the need arose, we would go over to each other, to finish off our tasks, assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it was normal within the headquarters for members of the staff to move around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not? When there was the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, as you know, this was a busy time for the headquarters, and I put it to you that it's simply inconceivable that you only saw three officers from the headquarters on the 12th and 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's how it was. I spent there for a short -- I spent a short space of time there. I spent far longer in a telephone conversation with the members of my family and the usual things you do when you're preparing for your activities the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On the 13th of July of 1995, was there any important news being discussed within the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My associates in the Press Centre told me that the operation around Srebrenica was winding up, and they were excited, they were pleased. They asked me what had happened on the front lines, where I had been with the units that I led at Treskavica, and I told them about what I knew: the positions of my own unit, the attacks, the casualties, our fighters who had succumbed, people we knew. They were interested in that, in hearing about that, and they helped me prepare some presents and some things that we were to take with us to Treskavica, some items.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you hear any news that morning that a column of able-bodied men, Muslims, had broken out of the enclave and were trying to make their way towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My associates in the Press Centre told me that they had heard over the radio. And I asked them whether there was any official confirmation of that, and they said no, they didn't. And that's where it ended. To be quite frank, I didn't actually believe that it was all true, that everything one heard over the radio was true, or the information by the Muslim radio. We didn't comment much about that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But that morning the Drina Corps headquarters received an order from General Gvero, who was the assistant commander for moral and legal affairs in the Main Staff, didn't they; they received an order in respect of this column of Muslims who were leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not acquainted with the order. Probably, because General Gvero was not able to contact -- that is to say, he didn't actually know that I was at the command headquarters -- corps headquarters, so I really don't know anything about that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you worked in the same branch as him, Witness, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but General Gvero knows that I was at Treskavica and not Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. The quality of the copy is not very good. Now, you can read it through briefly, but I'm principally interested in the first paragraph prior to the order. But if you wish, you can read it. Let me know when you're familiar with it. Now, you've read it and you see that news comes into the headquarters that hardened criminals and cutthroats who will stop at nothing in order to avoid capture and escape to the Muslim-controlled territory are making their way out of the enclave. Now, you will agree with me that when this order, this news, reached the headquarters, people must have been pretty excited and had been moving around quickly in order to do something about this; don't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this order arrived. I see it for the first time. And I maintain that in the headquarters and around the headquarters there was not too much excitement at all. In fact, I didn't notice any particular commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So could you explain to the Judges again the only information that you had on the morning of the 13th of July about the column of able-bodied men leaving the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat: My associates in the Press Centre conveyed the news to me from Muslim radio, broadcast over Muslim radio, that several thousand able-bodied men were allegedly breaking through towards Kladanj. As I say, I didn't actually believe the truthfulness of that report because during those days everything -- practically everything that was happening on the battlefront was tendentiously reported on, and I personally did not believe that it was true, under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But it's a rumour that, you would agree with me as a Staff officer at a military headquarters, people would check out and see whether or not it was true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I spent some time at the headquarters, I would quite certainly have checked it out. But as I say, I was moving around and my priority was to execute the order by the Corps Commander and Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you discuss the matter with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know whether he knew about it at this time? Did he know that the Muslim column had broken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything to me. Our conversation focused on my duties and responsibilities in keeping up morale and combat-readiness of the brigade at Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So am I fair in saying that, at this point in time, the only information that you had about the events in Srebrenica was your knowledge of the previous day of the headquarters mobilising transport for the movement of the refugees, and then this piece of information heard on the radio about the column breaking out towards Kladanj? That's the only information that you had on the morning of the 13th of July about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the only two pieces of information which I had about all the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And because you only saw three other officers in the headquarters, of course, naturally, you are unable to elicit any more information from other Staff officers, from operational Staff officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't even ask Jocic. I saw him going about his own business, and in the Operations Centre, we spent little time there unless we were just on duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying you'd also been told that the Srebrenica operation was winding down, that it was complete, by the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the guys at the Press Centre told me that Srebrenica was over, and I was happy to hear that because I didn't know of any -- that is to say, there was not too much information coming in. I said that all the information went via the Press Centre of the Main Staff, and so these guys here were not able to give me any more extensive information. As a man, as a human being, I was happy that, after the end of the operation, I could hope to see the units at Treskavica being reinforced, because I needed more men. Of course, this couldn't be done straight away. And so that's how that day ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But having these two pieces of information in your mind, were you not inquisitive to find out from other Staff officers in the headquarters what had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was inquisitive, yes, but I didn't have time. I had my own assignments and duties which I had to see to. And anyway, upon returning to the unit at Treskavica, via the Muslim television I learnt something more about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move ahead with the day of the 13th of July of 1995. You and General Krstic go to the military hospital together, and then I think you go on to visit your mother and then I think you go on to visit General Krstic's relatives. Can you tell the Judges the time that you were engaged in visiting these soldiers in the hospital and in visiting your family/relatives and General Krstic's relatives? What time of the day in the morning did you leave and what time did those events come to an end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I went to Sokolac before General Krstic, immediately after my conversation with him in the corridor. We met at about 11.30 at the Romanija Hotel at Sokolac, and we went off to the Main Staff hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, that evidence was clear. Just at what time of the day did you, I think, leave either General Krstic's relatives or your relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm saying. We got to the hospital at about noon; we met the doctors there, the surgeons. We toured the wounded, the injured, and talked to them, and that lasted for about --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is clear from your evidence and I want to move ahead. What time did you leave the hospital? What time did you finish visiting the soldiers and the doctors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 1430, 1500 hours, in that interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What time did you get to your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1530.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how long did you spend at your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had lunch, we stayed around -- well, perhaps it might have been an hour and a half at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long did it take to get to General Krstic's relatives from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 40 to 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you got to General Krstic's relatives at about 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little before 6.00, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long did you spend at General Krstic's relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a cup of coffee. Very short. Fifteen to twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then you went on to the forward command post at Krivaca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 1900 hours, before 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it just you and General Krstic in a single vehicle travelling together? Was there a driver? Was there an escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The driver was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the driver? Was it Krstic or Tosic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you talk about the operation in Srebrenica in the car with the General? I mean, you were with him for a long time in the car. Did you talk about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked more about my own position, that is to say, the position of my unit at Treskavica. That was what we discussed more than the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you say about Srebrenica? What did you talk about Srebrenica? Did you talk about the refugees being transported out of the enclave? Did you talk about the column of Muslim men that was escaping towards Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about that column escaping towards Kladanj very little. General Krstic was more concerned about the organised transport of the population. He was interested in whether my guys had conveyed the appeal for collecting the transportation vehicles, and that's it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General Krstic asked what help your unit could give in organising transport for the movement of the refugees from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit couldn't provide any assistance. We were very far away. Treskavica and Trnovo are 150 kilometres away, even 200 kilometres away from Srebrenica. And we had very specific assignments. I told you yesterday, we were exposed to very fierce fire, we had high casualties --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt. You stated, and I may have misinterpreted what you said, that "General Krstic was interested in whether my guys had conveyed the appeal for collecting the transportation vehicles." When you're referring to "my guys," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the two soldiers in the Press Centre who forwarded to the local radio stations. That's all I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General Krstic was checking with you whether or not the Press Centre had sent out the request for vehicles to be sent to Potocari to move the population to Kladanj and on to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krstic was not checking it out with me; he just asked me whether this appeal had been passed on to the local radio stations, which I confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you talked about the column with General Krstic, what did he say to you about that, when you briefly discussed that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me, "Let them pass, just so that this can be ended as it should," and I fully agreed with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the vehicle at the time, what communications arrangements were there in order for General Krstic to keep in touch with his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had radio communication, an RUP. I can't remember the number, the model. R-U-P.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this was how General Krstic kept in touch with the headquarters or that they could communicate with him whilst he made these social visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the standard method of communication whenever we were moving. However, I don't remember, at least not in my presence, that any communications were made. During those couple of hours, I don't remember that we communicated with anyone at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that General Krstic said to you about the Muslim columns, to let them pass. It was clear to you then, during that time, that he was well aware that a column of able-bodied Muslim men were breaking out of the enclave towards Kladanj; it was clear to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear from the conversation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, if you wish, perhaps it's an opportune time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Today we will change a little bit our timetable, because we used to break every 45 minutes for General Krstic. Now General Krstic is resting. We can resume our procedure and stay till 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are still --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm happy to keep moving ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence yesterday, Witness, that during the brief encounter that you had with General Zivanovic on the 12th of July, that he insisted that you go back to Treskavica immediately. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I may have misunderstood your testimony, but my understanding was, when you had the conversation with General Krstic outside his office in the headquarters, that he had said the same thing to you, that you should get back to Treskavica immediately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I should return immediately. But that didn't mean that very moment; it meant during the day. It's not so nearby that you can come and go so easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When General Krstic suggested that you go on these social visits to your relatives, did you tell him that General Zivanovic had stated to you that you were to return to Treskavica immediately because of the urgency of the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that in front of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he still stated that you should go on this social excursion to your relatives and his relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic knew that I had had a tragedy in the family several months prior to this, that my father had died. He had every understanding for me. And that is why he insisted, since I was there anyway, that I should visit my mother, who lived alone and who was normally very worried about me, which is quite understandable in view of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move ahead in time to the evening of the 13th of July. You had dropped off General Krstic at his forward headquarters in Krivaca and you then returned to Vlasenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you go to the corps headquarters in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to the press centre. I put in the vehicle, a Yugo 45, the supplies, the foodstuffs, and set off immediately for my destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges the distinction between Treskavica and Trnovo, or are they the same place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trnovo is a small town at the foot of Mount Treskavica. It is otherwise one of the municipalities of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday in your evidence that communication between Trnovo and Vlasenica was extremely difficult, and I'll quote exactly what you said: "Our communication with the command was made extremely difficult because of the combat operations that were ongoing in the broader area of Trnovo, so that we communicated via the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it was very hard to establish communication in that way." So I'm right in saying, based on your evidence, that it was extremely difficult to establish a communications link between Trnovo and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what the radio call sign was for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Was it "Bedem"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but it's a long time ago and there were many different names, so I really can't remember at this point in time. It could have been "Bedem." I do not exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Bedem" at least rings a bell that it could have been the call sign for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? You said yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in my mind the name is there, but I don't know whether that was it at that time. I really don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that, between the time that you went back to Trnovo and the 20th of July, that you had contacts with General Zivanovic on the radio. Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the radio. It was not possible to communicate by radio at such a distance. We could occasionally communicate by telephone and with a teletype device. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times did you speak with Zivanovic on the telephone between the 13th and the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I remember one of the conversations when the commander of the unit, Colonel Veletic, was at the observation post. Zivanovic called us, not me personally, but he asked for Veletic, requesting that we send the Chief of Staff of the 5th Brigade to his original unit because he was indispensable there to accomplish certain tasks probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the colleague in question was Vlacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that the only conversation that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the only conversation I had on telephone, but Veletic was more frequently on the phone as the unit commander. You must understand, we were with the troops on the front, to keep up morale and combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the telex machine, how many telexes do you recall coming from the headquarters at Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the number, absolutely not. It was never important for me to remember the number. It was important to carry out the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, we're actually now going to move to another area, so it may be an appropriate time, if you wish, to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. We can take a break until a quarter to eleven. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence wanted to make a kind of objection or, rather, to raise an issue which we did not have occasion to raise during the proceedings so far, but the Defence feels it is important regarding future planning of time for witnesses. The Defence examined this witness, according to my records, for about 90 minutes; Mr. Cayley has been cross-examining him for about 90, 95 minutes. I don't know how much longer he will need, but our understanding of the Rules is that the time for cross-examination should be roughly the same as the time devoted to the examination-in-chief. We just need instructions as to whether that Rule will be observed in the future so that we can plan the time for future witnesses, for the days ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. I quite share your opinion as far as time should be organised. We just should take into consideration that when you question the witness in the same language, apparently you can say more than when you have to speak a different language, and so on. So we can give an allowance of a few minutes, perhaps. But apart from that, I think we should be very much careful -- you have a rebuttal, and you can have it after that. But I'll ask Mr. Cayley. What are your plans?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, if I could comment, with your permission, Judge Riad, on what my learned friend has said. I do not believe that there is -- there is certainly not a written Rule within the Rules of Procedure that says that the length of time taken for the cross-examination must be equal to that taken by the examination-in-chief. I know that, on occasion, I think this Trial Chamber has desired that they be of similar length. But the reality is, cross-examination is a very different beast from examination-in-chief, and it is often necessary to make exploration into certain areas which, although not covered by the examination-in-chief, are nevertheless relevant for the case. I don't want to refer you to the Rules particularly, but Rule 89(H) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence makes that very clear, that the party -- the other party can make cross-examination not only into the subject matter of the examination-in-chief but also matters affecting the credibility of the witness and also whether the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party. Now, that may not be brought out by the other side, and the process of cross-examination may take a little bit longer. So that, in principle, is the view of the Prosecution. As far as this particular witness is concerned, I think I should be finished within an hour, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. We'll grant you an hour. And you have the chance for a rebuttal afterwards. Thank you. Mr. Cayley, you can proceed when he comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Cayley, let me ask you a question. Is it usually possible for you, before you hear the direct testimony of a witness, to make a reasonable estimate, based on what you know about what he's going to testify about? This comes up, as I know you're aware, where more and more we're putting pressure - not in this case particularly, in all cases - on both sides to estimate the amount of time that they're going to need, and clearly the Defence's time includes cross-examination. So it's useful sometimes to know ahead of time if it's going to be a day's cross-examination or two hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I'd make two points. As you know, Your Honour, we simply don't have access --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- to many of these people, as we do in domestic jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Secondly, the Prosecution is normally in the position where we only have the Rule 65 summaries. I mean, I don't wish to raise that as well, but in this particular instance, that summary bore little resemblance to what the witness actually said. I know, and I emphasise, that is not out of any policy of the Defence. That happened to them because they had difficulties in communicating with their witnesses. So I'm not suggesting it's anything to do with honesty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But nevertheless, that is why it is difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, surely by the time a witness has finished direct and you're getting ready to pursue your cross-examination, you must have some estimate as to whether it's going -- not to the minute but maybe to the half hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To the hour, I think, Your Honour. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To the hour. It might be useful at that point, maybe even for the Defence, if you have some notion, if you can share that with them or even with us, "I expect my cross-examination will be two hours," "three hours," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, we can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Krystal, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I just wanted to say, Mr. Cayley, when you spoke of Rule 89, it's actually Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I stand corrected. You're quite right. I was looking at 90 bis. It is Rule 90. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, could you please provide to the Judges the names of the other press officers who were working at the Drina Corps headquarters on the 12th and 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Risto Motika, Mitrovic Igor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where does Risto Motika live now in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mitrovic Igor, do you know where he lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I think he lives in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just one last point. When you were on the road with General Krstic on the 13th and you were talking with him about the problems in Trnovo, did you say to him that soldiers on the front needed a rest and needed to be rotated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were exhausted because they were constantly under fire. However, we insisted more, pursuant to the order of Colonel Veletic, on the replenishing of the unit with personnel rather than on the need for urgent rotation, because of the excess losses we were suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 811.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the commander of your unit, Witness, was Colonel Stojan Veletic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think the Chief of Staff, as you've already said, was Lieutenant Colonel Ljubomir Vlacic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the content of this order I'm not particularly concerned with; it's just the title of your brigade. Now, am I right in saying that on the 7th -- I think it says on yours, actually, the 6th. There's a mistake in the English translation. On the 6th of July, 1995, Stojan Veletic was the commander of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the name of that brigade was the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my notes, it says the 5th, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said to us yesterday that it was called the Podrinje Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was never so important to me. The important thing was the work that we did in the unit. It seems to me, as far as I can recollect -- I'm not sure -- that it was indeed the 5th Podrinje, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were a staff officer in a brigade which you can't clearly recollect the name of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was the 4th or the 5th doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What does it say at the top of this order? Can you read out to the Judges what it says, the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All members of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade are not allowed to move -- are banned from moving or loitering in the streets of Trnovo between 6.00 p.m. and 10.00 p.m. without a special order or permission from the Superior Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, because I think I perhaps gave you the wrong instructions. If you go to the top of the order where it says "Command," can you read out that line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Command of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And indeed, it's signed by the brigade commander, Stojan Veletic, at the bottom, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then it was probably the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that the name of the unit you were in was not the Podrinje Brigade but was, in fact, the 4th Drinski Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already stated in evidence to another question that I asked you that Ljubomir Vlacic was a member of the Birac Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that this brigade -- we now know officially that it was the 4th Drina Brigade -- was formed as a provisional unit, that is, a unit with a provisional composition consisting of elements of the Drina Corps and brigades from Sekovici; and the Chief of Staff, Mr. Vlacic, was named the Chief of Staff of the newly-formed unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in evidence that you recall a time after the 13th of July, 1995 when Lieutenant Colonel Vlacic left the Drina Brigade and went back to his own unit. Do you remember that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I think -- I think it was sometime around the 20th of July. I cannot recollect the exact date, but I know I have it noted down in my diary for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 364, volume 2. It's an intercept from the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to show you the transcript of an intercepted radio communication, and this is an intercept of a VRS radio communication. And I'm going to read it out. You can look at the Serbian version of it. It's tab 3. Now, Witness, if you recall, you do recollect that "bedem" was the call sign for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and let me read it out to you. It is a conversation that took place on the 17th of July, at 0910 hours, and the participants are X, bedem, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; Krstic; and Veletic, brackets (cannot be heard): "X: Hello, is that bedem? B: Yes. X: Listen Bedem, I need to talk to Colonel Veletic. B: I hear that for the first time, believe me. K: Bedem, Zlatar 01/ code name/ here, do you hear me? Over. B: Bedem speaking, go ahead. K: Give me Colonel Veletic from your IKM 3/forward command post/. B: Hold on a moment. K: Krstic here. B: Colonel Veletic is on the line, he can hear you. K: I can't hear him. Listen Bedem. B: Do you want me to pass it on to him? K: Listen Bedem. General Krstic is calling. B: Yes? K: Tell Veletic I ordered that Lieutenant Colonel Vlacic urgently return to the unit. B: Veletic says it's already been taken care of. K: It's been taken care of? B: Yes. K: So, he has to report urgently to the unit, he must be there by 1300 hours. B: He says everything's all right and it's already been taken care of. K: Has he left? Ask him. B: He's left already. K: Excellent. OK. B: Take care, goodbye." Now, Witness, you would agree with me that the contents of this intercept deal with the evidence that you've already given concerning the departure of Lieutenant Colonel Vlacic from the headquarters in Trnovo back to his unit in Birac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me that an individual by the name of Krstic is giving the orders to Colonel Veletic that Lieutenant Colonel Vlacic should return to his unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present during this conversation. Possibly those are the -- it may have taken place that way --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in that ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that the contents of this radio communication indicate that it was Krstic having a conversation with Lieutenant Colonel -- with, I'm sorry, Colonel Veletic rather than General Zivanovic, based on this piece of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Colonel Veletic was talking to. And I said that I had a conversation of similar contents with General Zivanovic who asked Veletic to go to his original unit. That's all I can say with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know of an individual by the name of Major Eskic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but I can't quite seem to remember his formation or establishment. You know, many people with many names went by during those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 808, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you see, Witness, that this is another order of the Command of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade; it's also signed by Colonel Stojan Veletic, Brigade Commander. Could you read out for the Judges paragraph 4 of that order? I'm sorry, once you've had an opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read out paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To all those who, at this decisive moment of our struggle, are counter to the aims to the struggle and do not carry out assigned tasks, the Command of the SRK shall take legal measures in accordance with the state of war declared in this territory against all those who, at this decisive moment of our struggle ..." et cetera. That is paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, you're aware that the SRK was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying that if the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was presented as the higher formation taking legal measures against members of the 4th Drina Light Infantry Brigade, that was your Superior Command whilst you were in Trnovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: We were the attached unit to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which is quite normal. We found ourselves in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had operational control over your unit and, in fact, had disciplinary authority over the soldiers in your unit, as far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in respect of these legal measures being taken against individuals who counter the aims of the Serbian struggle, are you aware of Serbs outside the Srebrenica enclave being prosecuted by the Serb authorities for assisting able-bodied Muslim men in escaping towards Tuzla? Are you aware of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, if we could for a moment move into closed session because we have two documents which mention the witness by name, and I'm going to need to read out portions of the document and that will identify him to the public. So if I can make an application for closed session, probably for about 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I assume you are agreeable, Mr. Visnjic? It's in the interest of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, it can be a private session, so that just the system is switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will read this intercept out to the Court. I'm not going to read all of it, I'm going to read approximately half of it, although Your Honours have seen this, and indeed I think we've read it out to you before. The conversation is between Colonel Cerovic and an individual named Vinko. Now, Colonel Cerovic is the Assistant Commander for Morale, Legal, and Religious Affairs within the Drina Corps; is that right, Witness? You have to make an audible response.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know of anybody within the Drina Corps called Vinko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who do you know? A senior officer called Vinko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I read out the intercept: "C: Colonel Cerovic wants to talk to him. : OK. C: Hello. V: Yes. C: Good morning Vinko. V: Good morning. C: How are you? V: Well, I'm running around since last night. We (went in?) again. C: Where? V: They are up there at Crni Vrh, over there at Potocani, Planinci, the part towards Baljkovica. C: Uh-huh. You mean the ones who are coming out on this side. Is that right? V: Yes, from there and all of them are rushing over here to us. C: You rushed off first. Rushed off. V: I really did, quite right. Well, yesterday we liquidated some 20-odd. C: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. V: And this morning we started chasing about 150 of them over there. There are in some kind of encirclement. C: And in which area are they surrounded? V: That's the Planinci-Baljkovica area. C: That means in the areas of Planinci and Baljkovica. V: Yes. C: You are good ... Vinko. V: Yes. C: What's your plan for tomorrow for shift replacement at Trnovo. V: I don't have a shift for Trnovo. C: Well, I know that was the order, that you've sent a report, however, this Eskic has just called me from up there and said that he was yesterday somewhere at your place and that he heard you are doing a shift rotation. V: No. I did a rotation of shift at Nisici. C: I'm telling you, the report he sent - there's not way it can be done ... That's Krstic's order, there are no shift rotations until further notice. V: It would be best if we transfer our complete Corps to the SRK/Sarajevo-Romanija Corps/." Now, I'm not going to read the rest of this document out. But you would agree with me, Witness, that the diary entry in the log, the war log, that I showed you, the 19th of July, in which the brigade command gives the order or expresses to the brigade that an order has been given for no shift rotations is, in fact, referring to this order, isn't it, Krstic's order that there be no shift rotations until further notice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see this as an order. This is a conversation by radio or by telephone, it doesn't matter; and from this conversation, all we can do is intimate that there was some hesitation as to whether it is possible to organise a shift at Trnovo or not, a replacement -- a rotation. You see that Mr. Cerovic would like to observe the order but he is objectively unable to do so, and the same applies to Vinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that Cerovic, in fact, states: "That's Krstic's order, there are no shift rotations until further notice." That is what Cerovic said in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, normally, because not only was there a problem now in our area of responsibility, but also in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that order for no shift rotation is the order that's referred to in the diary entry that we looked at a moment ago of the 19th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you originally spoke with Defence counsel about the evidence that you were going to give today, did you tell Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic that you had, in fact, stayed at the headquarters of the Drina Corps from the 13th to the 16th of July and that you were then sent to the front line at Treskavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You didn't say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I told you I kept a diary throughout the war for literary reasons, not for any reasons linked to this, and I have the precise data there. So I abide by what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when you told Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic that you had, in fact, been at the Vlasenica headquarters from the 13th to the 16th of July, that was prior to you checking your diary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because after all, that was so many years ago. One forgets a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you checked your diary, you, in fact, realised that you had left on the 13th of July, that you'd left for Trnovo on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, lastly and very briefly, Witness, you are aware of the allegations being made by the Prosecutor in this case, and all I wish to know from you is when you found out about information which is now public, which is now known by the entire world. When did you hear that upwards of 7.500 Muslim men had been executed within the Drina Corps' area of responsibility? When did you hear about that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the first information, where the numbers were much higher, from the Muslim media. I said that I didn't believe it, knowing full well what their propaganda was like. Regarding this particular case, I learnt after the arrest of General Krstic and his transportation here to The Hague, and I learnt this from the media, not from any official document, because I was no longer in the Staff or at the source of any information of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you only heard about this mass murder taking place very close to where you worked and lived when General Krstic was arrested and brought to The Hague. Prior to that, you had absolutely no conversations with any other Serbs or no access to any kind of reliable information about these killings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't have any reliable information. I did speak to the soldiers who took part in the operation. When I asked them whether it was true, what was being carried by the media, not one of them could tell me whether it was true. Why? Because all of them were on the move and all of them denied these figures, claiming that along the line of movement, they would come across some -- a few bodies of people who had been killed in conflict. As to the numbers, I really have no knowledge that 7.000 sparrows had died - it would have been visible - not to mention people, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned towards the end of your evidence a village within the area of the Romanija Brigade where I think you said that Muslims lived quite happily; I think the village of Vrbare. Do you recall your evidence on that? The inhabitants of the village of Vrbare, the Muslim inhabitants, stayed on throughout the war. I think you said that you were given orders by General Krstic to go and visit these people. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, indeed. I didn't get an order once but certainly more than ten times to go and tour those villages with Muslim populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did you stop touring those villages, the village in particular of Vrbare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always went to both Vrbare and Burati, but not so frequently when I was transferred to the Corps Command. At the end of the war, I left those areas. I know that all those people have survived and that they are grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you are not aware that in August of 1994 masked men began assaulting the village of Vrbare, and indeed a number, significant number, of the villagers in October of 1994 ended up in the Kula prison? You're not aware of that fact at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, and I sincerely regret it, if that is so, because these were people that I protected. I devoted so much attention to them that I am really sorry if that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Then it's time, perhaps, for a break of 45 minutes. We'll resume at 12.45. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would you like to resume?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Judge Riad. I've now finished my cross-examination. I think my learned friend Mr. Visnjic will have some re-examination, but I just wanted to raise two matters with the Court. First of all, I wondered what the timing was for the rest of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, we have to set that right in a way. I think we can have now a session till a quarter to two, a quarter-of-an-hour break, twenty-minutes break, and then resume till three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. And the second point was that I just wanted to remind the Court, and indeed the Defence: The agreement was, in respect of Defence witnesses, that Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Visnjic would be able to have contact with General Krstic during his examination, but that after General Krstic, the normal Rule would apply which applied to the Prosecution during its case in chief, that there would be no contact with the witness once the examination-in-chief had commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's what you applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is what was applied to the Prosecution. I was just simply -- because I know General Krstic has been testifying for a number of weeks, and I just wanted to state publicly that that was the understanding of the Defence, that they would have no contact with the witness -- with subsequent witnesses once they started testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Once they start.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the one who is here today --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If he doesn't come today, they can still contact him till Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Essentially, what I'm saying is this: Once a witness has started giving evidence in the courtroom, counsel will not have any contact with that witness. Obviously, prior to them giving their evidence, they can. I assume that's the Rule that's been applied, and indeed Mr. Visnjic is nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We all assume so. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have been applying that Rule, and indeed with the witness that has started his testimony, the Defence has had no contact with him since then, since testimony began. Therefore, I don't think there are any impediments there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Petrusic's response is as if I was accusing him, and I wasn't at all. I know, Mr. Petrusic, that you've had no contact. I just simply wanted to remind the Court that that was what we had agreed, because General Krstic had been testifying for so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The agreement is respected. But then there is another question for the next witness. Mr. Petrusic, would you like to, if we have time, to have the second witness today, or because that will deprive you of any contact ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the issue that we wanted to take up with the Prosecution, depending on how long their examination will last, and again depending on the questions by the Judges for this witness. The next witness that will be coming will not be examined for more than 45 to 50 minutes by the Defence, so I don't know how long -- but I don't know how long the Prosecution plans to examine that witness. And if we don't succeed by the end of the working day today, the Defence counsel would reserve the right to start off with an examination of the witness on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But my question went further. Are you in need still to have contact with the witness so that we'll not start before Monday, in the light of Mr. Cayley's reminder that you can never contact him after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we shall respect the Rule with respect to the witness and no contacts with the witness if testimony goes ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just clarify one thing? Do you want -- suppose we're through here in about an hour or less. I don't know how long your redirect is, but suppose we're through here in an hour or less. Do you want to begin the second witness today or would you rather wait until Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would rather get through the witness today, on condition, of course, that the Prosecution is able to finish the cross-examination of the witness that is coming next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I still can't get the right answer that I'm looking for. If we start on the second witness toward -- say in another hour or something like -- but we can't get all the way through the witness and the cross-examination today, would you rather not begin at all or go as far as we can go?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're putting me in a difficult position now. I have -- I fully respect the working hours of this Tribunal, of course, and we're ready to go ahead. But if the Trial Chamber has any obligations or our learned colleagues from the Prosecution do, then we would be ready to begin with that witness on Monday. But may I leave the decision to you, Your Honours? Perhaps I haven't been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One hour is an hour which I don't think the Court will find too taxing, and we don't want to extend working hours, of course, so this is a bit of a tricky situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, can I frame the question differently? Is there any emergency for the witness to go back before the weekend? We can make -- you can arrange perhaps -- you can ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. So proceed normally. Thank you very much. You are finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, do you have anything, or Mr. Visnjic? You would like to go to rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the spirit of this discussion, the Defence does not have any additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Judge Wald, would you like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just have two very brief questions, Witness DA. You testified that from the time that you left the Vlasenica headquarters on the 14th until I think you said around the 20th, you would still get communications of some sort from General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
