utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And what I wanted to know was whether or not through that entire period going up to the 20th, those communications were in his role as a general, or did they change at all? At what point did you become aware that General Krstic had been named as his successor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Mr. Zivanovic, how long he was a General. He's still a General today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How long General Zivanovic remained as commander of the Drina Corps. When you were getting communications from him all the way up to the 20th, did you see any change in his status during that period? That's the first question. The second is: When did you learn of General Krstic's successorship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as we received messages at Treskavica signed by General Zivanovic, for us he was the Corps Commander, for as long as he signed everything. The first message that we received with the signature of General Krstic, and that was sometime around the 20th -- I don't remember the exact date, whether it was a day or two before or after that date. So we received a message signed by the Corps Commander, General Krstic. On that same day, we sent out a congratulations message for his appointment as commander to Commander Krstic on behalf of the fighters of the 4th Drina Brigade and in the name of the command of that unit as well, the commanding staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you do -- or do you remember receiving communications from General Zivanovic which were either labelled or on their face were communications he was making as the chief of the -- as the commander of the Drina Corps right up until the 20th? Do you remember specifically whether you got any, or what those were? In the latter days, in the latter days of that period. You left on the 13th, I guess it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the latter days of that period, that is to say, sometime around the 20th, we received messages by teletype where Zivanovic was interested in the state of affairs as regards morale and the combat-readiness of our unit, and they were still signed, "Corps Commander, General Zivanovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second last question is: When later on you did learn of the allegations, I'll use that word for here, the allegations of the mass executions of the Srebrenica column, and also in some cases of the refugees, and according to your own testimony recently, you knew that the Drina Corps had been engaged during this period in mopping-up operations or in trying to find and capture the columns, what was your reaction at that point? I mean, what did you think when you put those two things together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I was not able to believe that our forces could carry out an assignment of that kind, because I knew that perhaps just 1.500 fighters could be engaged in that operation. I wondered how these people managed, with an enemy that was 15 times stronger and well-armed, how they managed to overcome such an enemy, and I was more prone to believe, as I was not on the terrain itself, that everything had taken place on the basis of an agreement of some kind, whatever you like to call it. When you ask me when I learnt of the sufferings of that column, I said that the first information reached us from the Muslim information media, and those figures were really exaggerated, almost to the extent when it was said that Zepa has a population of 40.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But what about later on? Even after the events were mostly over and you learned that, in fact, it appeared that these massacres/executions had taken place - had taken place - what was your reaction then? I know you have great honour, respect, and perhaps love for the Drina Corps, but on the point of learning that these things, there was strong evidence they had actually happened, and you had not been on the terrain but you'd been in the area and you knew many of the personalities involved, what was your feeling/reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even then, not even at this moment am I able to believe it all. I am first and foremost a humanist by vocation and choice, and quite simply because of those people and because of the honourable officers of the Drina Corps, I do not wish to believe it, and I cannot believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you do not believe it at present? You do not believe it at present?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's the wrong one. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't wish to believe it, neither can I, being who I am, the personality that I am, can I believe all that. If it truly did happen, then I am profoundly sorry because I spent the whole war working to save people. I indicated the need to coexist, cohabit, to love one another, love man, and that is my life-long option, generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sure we all share that, except at times reality intrudes upon some of our desires. But if those were your feelings, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Wald. Witness DA, good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to understand a few things from you. The first thing concerns your competence/jurisdiction. You were the Assistant Commander for Morale, Religious, and Legal Affairs in the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, and in fact, apparently, you took action against one of your officers, Major Suka, because he led the units of the Palija Battalion into the Redjani Gorge where about 60 men were killed. So you were taking action against officers who committed grave violations. Did you take any action, you or your department, concerning the violation of human rights or war crimes at any moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that as against Major Suka action was taken, and it is still ongoing; the legal proceedings have still not been concluded. All that happened at the beginning of the war operations and immediately before General Krstic came to the 2nd Romanija Brigade. If you're asking me whether we took action of any kind, took steps of any kind, with respect to the events that are topical here, that are being discussed here, then I should like to inform Your Honours that at the beginning of August, upon my return from my assignment at Treskavica, at the request of the civilian authorities from the Corps Command, following permission from General Krstic, the Commander, I went to my work assignment and I became a professor at the gymnasium, the secondary school, because they needed teaching staff for work in the field of education in Republika Srpska. The Legal Department in the Corps, which was made up of lawyers Lubez and the late Marijanovic, I do not know whether the department did anything along those lines, took any action. Because after my departure from the Corps, I saw Marijanovic only once while he was lying in hospital at the clinical centre in Belgrade, and as he was seriously ill, I did not ask him anything about the subjects we are discussing here and now. Therefore, I have no knowledge as to whether the Legal Department of the Corps took any steps or not in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also were in very -- I believe, in friendly contact with General Krstic. Did he mention to you that he ordered any investigation or any action concerning, at any moment, violations of human rights or war crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my departure to take up my duties, I rarely saw General Krstic. Perhaps we had a little more time on one occasion to talk and to exchange information about each other's families and what the future held for us in peacetime, what we were to do in peacetime. The most important thing for me was to forget the war; I am trying to wipe it out of my recollections as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, there was some kind of, what can I say, contradiction between your going with General Blaskic on this -- with Krstic on this social errand and the order you received from General Zivanovic on the 12th of July to return to your unit, because if I gather rightly, you received this order from Zivanovic on the 12th of July, and on the morning of the 13th, General Krstic asked you to accompany him. Whose orders are you supposed to obey? Who was in charge then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Commander, General Zivanovic, did not insist that I return that very same moment to my original unit, but he did not allow me to stay for several days either. He was reasonable and understood my need to return the next day to take up my assignments; the Chief of Staff, General Krstic, had a complete understanding of that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in the army, I think orders are orders. I mean, when you are ordered to return to your unit, either Zivanovic was in power, either he had authority, or he didn't. So at that date, were the orders of Zivanovic, more or less, weaker than the orders of General Krstic or, let's say, inexistent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. Subordination was respected fully to the end where we come from. General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander, but he didn't write me a letter with an order; he didn't issue a written order or an oral order. But as human beings, we reached an agreement that I should return to my unit the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How long did this errand last, your social and family visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family or the visit with General Krstic's family?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Your being with General Krstic off and on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We visited the wounded and stayed there for about two hours; then we spent about an hour and a half with my mother and perhaps half an hour or a little longer with his relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And wherever you are, you are in close contact with the media and the information. Was it difficult to get information of what was happening? Were you completely cut off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a great extent. There was a lot of combat activity in the Treskavica area, and very frequently the telephone communications were down. We had almost exclusively to rely upon the information media of the Bosnian Muslims and, to an extent, Serbian radio, for as much as it could be heard in those regions, because it wasn't strong enough. The transmitters weren't strong enough to relay it always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you gave no credit to the information coming from the Muslim media? When you said that you knew from them about the massacres, about mass murder, and so on, would you take that as a lie, or you would give it consideration and check it, you and the whole ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it to be untruths, learning from the Markale experience, and many others as well. Therefore, I had reason not to believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the word was spread; everybody knew. Whether it's wrong or right, the information passed, wherever it's coming from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian language, rumours, I mean something that has not been checked out and established as truth, and that is how we took it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, speaking about information, and you mentioned that the soldiers were furious because they knew about the -- what you called the Christmas massacre, and other things there. And who spread the word and who really -- in your opinion, where did they get this information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. I spoke about the massacre that occurred on Christmas 1993, and then it was the relatives of precisely the fighters who were in my unit who lost their lives. So you must understand that they wanted to rid themselves of the presence of the people who were, until yesterday, their neighbours and in the encirclement around their villages, because there were many dead on the Serbian side before the war ended, especially in Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to know: To keep the morale of -- because you were apparently also commander for morale. To keep the morale high and the desire to fight strong, was there some kind of propaganda telling the people how their enemy -- what their enemy did and how they should take revenge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We cautioned the fighters exclusively of the need to hold the front lines in the Treskavica and Trnovo area, and there was no kind of propaganda whatsoever. We did not spread any kind of propaganda, nor was there any need to do so. We pointed out to them the fact that their co-fighters from the units were doing their best to do -- to liberate Srebrenica even without them, and although many of them had a fervent wish to be down there at the time. Of course, they were concerned and worried about their families and their houses, because the Muslim forces were moving around in the area, in precisely that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think my last question: You mentioned that General Krstic said once, concerning the column, the Muslim column, "Let them pass ..." I'm quoting your words, "Let them pass so that it could end as it should," the Muslim column breaking out of the enclave towards Kladanj. When he said, "Let them pass," he is a general. Did such an order be obeyed or was it wishful thinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, a different order from the distinguished officer I could not have expected, and this is the first time that I'm hearing that kind of formulation, but where the officer could say nothing else but to let the column pass and everything to pass, not only the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't exactly understand. When he said, "Let them pass," did they pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in the area. I was not in the area. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whom was he saying that to? Was it to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no need for him to say it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, you said that he said, "Let them pass so that it could end as it should." I would like to know more details about -- if you said it, I quoted it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no audible response from the witness. We didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little mixed up now. As I say, I wasn't in the area when those events took place. There was no movement of columns in the sector where I was. As you have read out, it referred to the sector of the zone of responsibility of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just some exhibits, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you can liberate our witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, I thought we should do it in the presence of the witness in case there are any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The first exhibit is 804, A and B, which is actually the same as the previous exhibit, which was Exhibit 402/3, tab 7. So that's an exhibit that's previously been admitted that has been renumbered, and that's now renumbered as 804A and B, the English and the original Serbian version. Then Exhibit 805, which is the Mladic and Karadzic indictment. Then Exhibit 811, A and B, which is the Drinski Brigade order. 808, A and B, another Drinski Brigade order. And then 815, which -- A and B, the original and the English version. That's the war log from the Zvornik Battalion of the Drinski Brigade. And then 810, A and B, which is the other battle diary from the Drinski Brigade. I would apply for 815 and 810 to be placed under seal because the -- both of those documents contain reference to the witness by name, and if they are under seal, that essentially ensures that his identity is not revealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Defence counsel, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So let it be. I'd like to thank you, Witness DA, and wish you a safe trip back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. It was an honour for me to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has a new witness. So the usher is not here for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you ask for any special measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll wait for the usher to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the General has just informed me that he is suffering some pains, so if we could make a brief break or if he could be allowed to leave the courtroom briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You must have heard me speak to Judge Wald. I was telling her the same thing. I was suggesting that we have a small break and General Krstic can rest a little bit. But it will be a quarter of an hour, and then we'll have no break till we finish your witness. Is that all right with you? Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to ask the usher to be kind enough to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. You will be asked now to take the oath that is right before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. You can sit down. The witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friends of the Prosecution, we have before us Zeljko Borovcanin, Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Borovcanin to tell us his name for the record, rather, his surname, to spell it out, as has been done in the proceedings so far.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: B-O-R-O-V-C-A-N-I-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, will you tell us briefly when and where you were born, where you lived, your short biography?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I was born on the 19th of April in 1958, village of Zunovi, Sokolac municipality. I completed four years of primary school in my native village. From there I went to Sarajevo, to Pofalici --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon for interrupting you, Mr. Borovcanin. I know that you're a little bit nervous. Please relax, take it easy, and I would like to ask you to speak slowly because of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I understand. After completing four years of primary education, I went to Sarajevo, where I completed secondary school of commerce, eight years of education. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In 1977, I went to do my military service in the former Yugoslav People's Army; in 1979, I returned from the army and I found a job in special purpose industry in Sarajevo, in Vogosca. I got married. I have two children. We lived in Sarajevo, in Pofalici; I had a house of my own there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The war in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina started in April 1992. Where were you when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, when the war started, I was in Sarajevo, in Pofalici, together with my family. At the beginning of April, barricades were put up, and from that moment on I was unable to go to work; we were surrounded on all sides, I mean Pofalici as a settlement, until the 15th or 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Pofalici as a locality, was it inhabited by both Muslims and Serbs and Croats? Was it a mixed population?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When I moved there 20 years ago, the population was majority Serb; but for the last ten years prior to the war, large numbers of people came to settle there from Sandzak, so that, just before the war broke out, the majority population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So in mid-May, you left your place of residence. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 16th of May when the attack started, together with my family and the other refugees - a total of 1.000 people - across the Hum relay point, I managed to reach free territory under the control of the Serbs. About 200 people were killed in Pofalici, mostly women, children, and old people who did not manage to escape across this Hum mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said you reached Serb territory. Where? Which territory? Just please speak slowly and make pauses between the questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Via Hum we got to Zuc, territory controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it in Zuc that you joined the army of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. We just spent the night there. Because we reached Zuc in the evening, we spent the night. In the morning, the whole group of refugees went on towards Vogosca, and I was with them together with my family. From there I went to Zunovi, my native village, and on the 18th, in the evening, I reached Zunovi and my parents' house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the army of Republika Srpska? And if so, when did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When I arrived in the village, two or three days later I was drafted to the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I was a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about May 1992. Did you remain in that unit until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When I arrived in my native village, and after I was mobilised, as a line of separation had not been established yet, my village was surrounded and the members of the army stayed in the village until a line was formed in Krusevo. That is when we went to the lines held by the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So would you agree that, until the end of the war, you were a member of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade until the end. But in 1994, I joined a reconnaissance platoon of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But that platoon was part of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us now go on to July 1995. So at the beginning of July 1995, where were you or, rather, your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: At the beginning of July 1995, my unit was near the Olovsko Theatre, the locality called Ajdinovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So that was a fortified position, defence position? What kind of a position was it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: It was a defence position, but we, as the reconnaissance platoon, were there as reinforcements on the line because of attacks by Muslim forces, because the line was not a very firm one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So how long did you stay there in those positions at Ajdinovici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact dates. I said that in the preparations for my testimony. But I think it was the 3rd or 4th of July that we got orders from our commander to report to headquarters of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said Palez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. Knezina. Knezina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are those two localities close to one another?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Right next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the command, did you receive any orders, any assignments?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Our commander told us that we should be ready for the next day because we would be going towards Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you get any more detailed instructions or guidelines?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That next day, the day that followed the day you arrived at headquarters, did you start towards Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We started towards Zeleni Jadar the next day and we arrived in the evening. We set up our tents and we spent the night there. Let me just add that we were reinforced by another 30 men from the front line, and my reconnaissance platoon numbered about 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So from Knezina was it 30 plus 30 men that set off?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: About 60 men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you set up camp, did you set up camp in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. We set up camp there and spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Among the command staff, as this was the 2nd Romanija Brigade, was any staff officer present?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The commander of the reconnaissance platoon, the late Milenko Bojovic, and the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So who was the commander of your reconnaissance platoon?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The late Milenko Bojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please make pauses after my question. Can you tell us what date that was when you were there at Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I think it was the 5th to the 6th that we spent the night at Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Once there, did you or your unit receive any more detailed information as to why you were there, from your commander, and what your concrete assignment was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Talking to the commander, I learnt that -- and so did the other members of the reconnaissance platoon -- that we needed to capture certain features around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Preparing for this testimony, you told us which elevation points you were -- your unit was supposed to gain control of, so will you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Alibegovac, which we reached and we spent the night there, and we thought that was the end of it, the end of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But before you reached Alibegovac, did you engage in any combat, that is, from the moment you arrived to the Zeleni Jadar region until you reached Alibegovac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th, I think it was, that we went on a reconnaissance mission towards Jasenovo and Kiprovo. We spent that day reconnaissance duty. We came across a minefield. And then we went back to Jasenovo and we stayed there for two or three days. I think it was until the 9th of July, because the weather was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the way to Kiprovo, or rather Alibegovac, did you encounter any resistance by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We had some minor resistance at Kiprovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you encounter UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When we passed Kiprovo, there's a slope there that was covered in woods. When we got to the edge of the wood, there was a field there, and on that field we saw a checkpoint held by UNPROFOR which was fenced in with barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you open fire against UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No, because we had received strict orders that we must not fire at UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you gain control or capture, I mean in military usage, that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: As I said, when we reached the edge of the wood down there, we saw that there was an observation post within the compound of the UNPROFOR forces, and from that observation post, looking through our binoculars, we saw the UNPROFOR soldier waving to us to approach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We stopped there for a moment, because you know how it is, and maybe five or ten minutes later we went forward. When we crossed the field, we saw him waving to us to keep to the left-hand side, which we did. We came to the entrance of the checkpoint and we stopped there. There were three of us: the commander and two of us soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with the UNPROFOR soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Since the commander could speak English, I think that their commanding officer came out. They established contact. And we soldiers were not allowed to go in, nor to have any contact with UNPROFOR soldiers. Afterwards, I learnt from the commander that, before us, Muslim forces had been there which had pressured the Dutch Battalion forces which had been stationed there, and that they had killed one of their soldiers, forcing them to shoot at us so that they could withdraw more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that there was communication between your commander and the commander of that UNPROFOR post. What kind of contact was it? A conversation? Was it -- when you said "contact," tell us what you meant.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: A conversation. They talked. Because we had strict orders if we come across UNPROFOR forces, that we must not shoot, that we must not seize their sidearms or equipment, and the agreement was that those troops should be escorted towards Bratunac, that is, the UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you escort them to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We soldiers in front of the checkpoint took control of the trenches which had previously been held by the Muslims, and people were designated to accompany them towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they hand over to you their personal weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: While I was there, no, but I heard that they were escorted, together with their personal weapons and equipment, to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So as a member of this reconnaissance platoon, you were, one could say, a forerunner of the rest of your unit which was following you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That was our purpose. That was our duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So when you reached this post at Alibegovac, was there any shelling from heavy weapons that used shells as ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No, because it wasn't necessary anyway, as the Muslims were withdrawing, retreating.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand you, you and your unit reached that position without any significant resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Mr. Petrusic. Judge Riad, I'm sorry. Could we just have a date? I know -- are we still talking about the 9th of July? Because many events have happened. I just wondered where we were at the point when the witness said that there was no shelling. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Mr. Cayley. In my next questions we will come to the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So my question was: When you reached this position at Alibegovac, there was no serious conflict with your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, could you tell us when you reached this position held by UNPROFOR, that is, Alibegovac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 9th of July, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you move forward on that same date, or rather, what did your unit do next?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 9th, in the evening, we reached the line assigned to us and the commander gave us orders to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the next day, the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, we received orders from the commander to head towards the settlement of Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Throughout this period, from the 6th of July until the 10th of July, in the morning, were you aware of who your neighbours were on your right-hand and left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We did. We had to. That was our duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was on your right and who on your left?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the right was the Birac Brigade and on the left the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So they, too, have their own axis of attack.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive orders from on the 10th of July, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We received all orders from our commander, the late Branko Bojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who gave him orders?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We soldiers only knew about our own commander. As to who he got his orders from, that for us meant a superior level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would it be logical that if you were part of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, that your commander received orders from the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, correct, from the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So let us go back to that order or, rather, your next assignment on the 10th, in the morning, the attack towards Slapovici. Would you explain to us what happened on the way to Slapovici. Did you engage in any combat?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When we reached the outskirts of Slapovici, a group was designated to reconnoitre and see whether there were men there or Muslim forces. A group of us, four or five, entered the village of Slapovici, passed through it and came out on a hill overlooking Slapovici. There was absolutely no one around. We gave the sign. There was some hay or something, I don't know exactly, but we set fire to it, and we gave the signal that the rest of the unit could pass through safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As you passed through Slapovici and, if you know, when the rest of the unit passed through, was there any torching of the village of Slapovici, torching of houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. There weren't any, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was there artillery support that shelled facilities in Slapovici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: There was no need because Slapovici had already been abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So after passing through Slapovici, you reached the feature you called Brdo. Can you tell us anything more about that feature, to define it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: It's a little hill; I really don't know whether it has a name. Because when we reached Brdo, there was resistance by the Muslim forces. That was the strongest resistance that we encountered in the course of the operation along our axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the 10th of July. Could you roughly tell us what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I think it was about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you continue the attack? What happened with your unit when you reached that point?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The unit went on, went forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly where you got to by the end of that day, the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When we left Slapovici, we reached the asphalt road, and I think it leads from Zeleni Jadar towards Srebrenica. We moved on for awhile and then we stopped and spent the night there. We stopped for the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you reached the road, Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica, was there any resistance by the BH army there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So your unit stopped for the night there, that is, the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next day, the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, in the morning, we were given orders to march along the left-hand side of the road. There was a valley there, that we should go 'round it, because from a position - I think it's called Bojna - there was an artillery piece firing so we couldn't go on. Our reconnaissance unit started, and around 12.00 or 1.00, it captured that elevation point as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said there was a Browning firing. A Browning, is that a large-calibre weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 11th of July, were there any NATO air strikes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We were in the valley. We heard the explosions but we didn't know what it was. Later on, we learnt that these were air strikes against our targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you or, rather, your unit enter Srebrenica on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that your unit was at the locality Bojna at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Maybe two or three soldiers left without permission of the commander, but in the evening, we were all there at Bojna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That is where you were during the night between the 11th and the 12th, so did your unit stay there for the night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, did you receive any orders from your commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, we were given orders by the commander to move, to search the terrain in the direction of Jahorina, Viogora, and there was a third place whose name escapes me just now. That is where the units were to assemble; to search the terrain on the way there and to assemble there. Suceska was the third locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now that you've said Suceska, you are talking about the search and assembly in the area of Jahorina, Viogora, and Suceska.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did your unit assemble there on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It wasn't just us. There was the Zvornik and also the Birac Brigades that assembled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the commanders of those units, were they there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. But I do know that when we got up there we were all tired. We had Dr. Zugic, and our leader conveyed to him that we were tired and that there were some people suffering from a skin disease. The skin of their feet had split. And after that the order was received that we ought to line up and that we would be addressed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did General Mladic address you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: He addressed us and said on the occasion that we were to go to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you be certain, although in the course of our talk with you so far -- can you be certain as to the day when General Mladic addressed you? When was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I said then, as far as the date is concerned when we had our conversation, that I just know that it was the entry into Srebrenica and the search of the terrain. And as to the General Ratko Mladic's address to us, whether it was on the 12th or the 13th, in the morning, when we moved off to Zepa, I can't be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After that search of the terrain and the assembly of your unit and the other units, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We went back to Jasenovo, where we started out from and where our tents were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You are mentioning the Jasenovo for the first time now. Is it the Zeleni Jadar area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I forgot to say that the tents from Zeleni Jadar were transferred to Jasenovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollections, this was on the 13th when your unit moved onwards towards Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which route your unit took?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Our unit, I know for certain, did not pass across Srebrenica, Potocari, because we would have got out onto the road which leads from Konjevic Polje, Kasaba - and that is something that we know from earlier on - but it took a different route. And that was the first time that I ever passed that way myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you reached the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We arrived in the evening, and it was the Plana area where we spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Plana area is the broader environs of Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the other units? Had they arrived there too?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They were arriving. It was already getting dark and everybody fended for themselves; where they found themselves they spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, in the morning, if I follow you - you were speaking of the 13th - but on the morning of the 14th, where were you and your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the morning of the 14th, we received orders to move to Pozepje [phoen], whether it was a school or a shop. But we were supposed to be the reserve for the Zvornik Brigade somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You say "the reserve for the Zvornik Brigade." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade held the main axis of the combat line towards Zepa, and because we were tired, we were left to stand as a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, in the morning, we received the order to replace the Zvornik Brigade which had to return to its command headquarters, and we took up its axis and line. And I later learnt that it had to return because of the breakthrough of the Muslim forces from Srebrenica towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said you learnt later on, "We learnt later on that this was because of the breakthrough of forces." Did you learn anything more about that or was that just a piece of information along the usual lines?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That's all we learnt. We heard that. Nobody actually informed us. We heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, briefly, let us move on. You entered that main axis and the fighting towards Zepa lasted in continuity?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During that time, during the time you spent there, that is to say -- let me rephrase that. Who issued you orders?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: All orders to the reconnaissance platoon were issued by our leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that time frame, that is to say, during those fighting operations towards Zepa, did you see General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. He would come frequently to tour the line and to visit us fighters, particularly those of us who were in the main section of the combat operations, main theatre of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When he visited you, did he address the commanders personally, the leaders, the fighters? Whom did he address?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, he talked to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Krstic was the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade at the time when you were a member of that brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: In 1992, in the place of the brigade commander, instead of Veljko Bosanac, General Radislav Krstic came and he stayed up until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet him more frequently during that period?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: He was with us fighters all the time up at that part of the Olovo battleground. He spent most of his time there and lost his leg there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During the time that he commanded the brigade, do you happen to know whether there were any prisoners of war in the command of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: As I live in Knezina as a refugee, a displaced person, I know that there were some Muslims captured who were put up in Knezina in a building there. They were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What was the treatment towards those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They ate the same food that the army ate which was in Knezina. They received cigarettes. And I had occasion to talk to them as well. They were satisfied. Nobody mistreated them in any way. And they left. I don't know exactly when. But I did have occasion after the war to meet a man who had been detained there and to say hello to the General, the man who was in prison. He told me to say hello to the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: The surname Borovcanin, is that a common surname? Is it rare in those parts or is it a common, widespread surname?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Half of Romanija -- half the people in Romanija have the surname Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just take a moment to confer with my colleague, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that that superior level of command, that you weren't well acquainted with it. That would be the essence of your answer to one of the questions I asked. But my next question has precisely to do with that. Do you have any knowledge, and if so, when did you come by that knowledge, as to when General Krstic became the commander of the corps, of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Let me just answer your previous question. When I said that I had no insight into that, into superior levels of command, I meant in combat operations, as regards combat operations. That's what I had in mind. And General Krstic -- I learnt that later on, after returning from Zepa to the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. That was at the beginning of August -- he took up the post of commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So your knowledge of that dates back to his appointment after you came back to the brigade headquarters in Knezina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether, in the course of the combat activities around Zepa, so that we don't have to go back to that again, whether there were any prisoners of war taken in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Along our axis there was not, but as negotiations were underway and as our unit was frequently stopped in our combat activities to let a Muslim delegation pass through towards negotiations, they always had time to withdraw to their reserve positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you received orders to cease the fighting, to stop your combat activities, when, as you say, delegations were supposed to pass through on their way to the negotiations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who issued those orders?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Mostly those orders were issued by our leader, but on one occasion, and that was by the Purtici area, when I heard on the Motorola General Krstic issuing a strict order that all hostilities be stopped to let a delegation pass which was moving from Zepa, from the relay, that is to say, towards Zepa, to attend negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you and your unit, during the fighting that took place at Srebrenica and Zepa, did you receive instructions from the command as to how you should behave, what your conduct should be towards the civilian population and towards prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Every battalion had the officer in charge of moral guidance, and he spent all his time with us. And we would receive orders from our commanders and our leaders as to how we should behave in the case of prisoners of war being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify the term. I know what you mean by "the officer in charge of moral guidance." In our own language we know what it means, but let's explain. It is an individual dealing with legal, religious, and other affairs linked to the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this completes the examination of this witness by the Defence, my examination of Witness Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Now, Mr. Cayley, do you think you can do that today?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Not in 15 minutes, Judge Riad, no. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would you like to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you wish, I can start today and use the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that you were born on the 19th of April, 1958, in Zunovi in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you've already said in your evidence in chief that you lived in Sarajevo for a number of years. How old were you when you moved to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I attended fifth form in Sarajevo, so that was in 1969. And since then, I have spent all my life in Sarajevo, that is to say, up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you lived in Sarajevo until the war began, essentially?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Up until the 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that you lived in a street called Humska Street?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the number of your house? 210?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your job at the factory that you spoke about? Were you a lathe operator?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I worked in the factory that made ball bearings, UTN. On a lathe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: In Vogosca, near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Radomir Riscevic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Gornji Pofalici, were you engaged yourself as a volunteer in any Serbian defence units in that place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me again the date on which you joined the 2nd Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The 2nd Romanija Brigade, I was mobilised into it on the 20th or the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of which month?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in 1995 what was the name of the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade in July 1995 was Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. We have to adjourn immediately. There is an alarm in the Tribunal. Everybody has to leave in good peace and order. And we'll adjourn until Monday morning, 9.20. So please leave the courtroom.
